summary:
Uttarakhand has no trans-specific statute, enforcement series or documented incident pattern of its own, and the national framework of India applies in the state without material deviation. Nothing in the sourced record indicates a divergent state policy, so a trans visitor to Uttarakhand should expect the national legal position to govern encounters with police, documents and public services.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex persons, and requiring medical certification of identity. Human Rights Watch, reporting on 26 March 2026, describes the amendment as reversing the 2014 Supreme Court ruling that had established self-identification. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Presidential assent was still pending in late March 2026; Human Rights Watch urged the president not to sign, and a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the bill, calling the removal of self-identification a setback against the 2014 ruling.

The amendment adds offences carrying penalties of up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender. Human Rights Watch warns that this provision could criminalise the support networks on which trans people rely.

Recognition coverage is narrow in practice. Of 487,803 transgender persons recorded in the census, roughly 32,500 hold identity cards, against a wider national estimate of about two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The government presents the March 2026 amendment as widening access to welfare schemes and anti-trafficking protection by narrowing who qualifies. Critics, among them rights activist Akkai Padmashali, describe it as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, arguing that it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people.

The gap between census-recorded trans people and identity-card holders suggests that even those inside the recognition scheme rarely hold the documents that the new certification process governs. Whether the medical boards and district authorities introduced by the amendment have begun operating in Uttarakhand is not addressed in the sourced material.

The 2024 transition from the Indian Penal Code to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is reported alongside the checkpoint incidents as a compounding factor: trans communities describe both a loss of specific legal shields and a heightened fear of assault in practice.
localsOnly:
Residents of Uttarakhand seeking legal recognition of gender identity now face a certification route rather than self-declaration: medical boards and district authorities must certify gender-affirming surgery, and recognition is anchored to traditionally accepted socio-cultural identities plus biological or physical traits.

The Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police bind police conduct nationally, including in Uttarakhand: they direct police sensitisation, prohibit conversion therapy, and instruct the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Residents who encounter police harassment can invoke these directions, and the Allahabad High Court, which has jurisdiction over Uttarakhand, granted relief to a trans passport applicant in February 2026.

Welfare-scheme eligibility for residents is tied to the narrowed definition of transgender person introduced in 2026, which the government says concentrates benefits on historically recognised groups and trafficking victims.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Uttarakhand-specific incident, arrest, court filing or enforcement pattern involving trans people is sourced; the state-level assessment rests entirely on the national framework and on incidents recorded elsewhere in India.

The status of presidential assent on the March 2026 amendment was unresolved in the sources as of late March 2026, and no later material confirms whether the bill was signed, amended or challenged.

The census figure of 487,803 transgender persons and the separate estimate of about two million are not reconciled in the sources; the basis for either count is not stated.

Whether the certification machinery created by the 2026 amendment has been implemented in Uttarakhand, and how district authorities there process applications, is not sourced.
